items: Unbounded spawning.
One goroutine per incoming item, no limit.
A traffic spike becomes an OOM.
Bound it with a pool, semaphore, or `SetLimit`.

blocks.text: A hard exit runs no deferred cleanup in any goroutine. Same for `main` returning — every other goroutine dies mid-flight.

Before Go 1.23, `time.After`'s timer was not collected until it fired — a real leak in a hot `select`. Since Go 1.23 unreferenced timers are collected immediately, so the remaining cost is one allocation per iteration; `time.NewTimer` + `Stop` or `context.WithTimeout` still avoids it.
Use `time.NewTimer` + `Stop`, or `context.WithTimeout`.

blocks.title: The whole handbook in one line
blocks.text: Goroutines are cheap because the runtime schedules them M:N over threads with 2 KB copying stacks — and they stop being cheap the moment one blocks with no way out.

caption.text: Part 2 of GO GOROUTINES. A goroutine costs 2 KB and about a microsecond — until one blocks forever, and then it costs you a stack, its captured variables, and eventually the pod. This handbook walks the whole runtime: G/M/P, what `schedule()` does 61 ticks at a time, how stacks grow by copying, the nine ways goroutines leak, and the pprof ladder for finding them. Save it for the next time RSS climbs while your heap stays flat.
